body_markdown:
It is, arguably, the most exclusive seat in motoring. The S-Class you have to apply to buy, but will never drive yourself. The new Mercedes-Benz Guard: the ride of choice for paranoid heads of state worldwide.


A big black Merc has been the ride of choice among world leaders for nearly a century. These four-doors have ferried every kind of figurehead from the democratic to the despotic, as our[recent story on dictators’ wheels](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/cars-owned-by-dictators-almost-everything-youd-ever-want-to-know/) outlined. These people don’t drive themselves, of course. It’s the rear that represents the true seat of power, occupied by world leaders with every conceivable title, from Colonel Gaddafi and Emperor Hirohito to Chairman Mao and the Pope (prior to the Popemobile).


Mercedes-Benz


Those who lead a car-producing nation like the U.S. must be seen to support the home team with their choice of wheels. (Since G.W. Bush’s presidency, America has seen a number of Caddies nicknamed “The Beast”.) But those who don’t have mostly defaulted to an armored Mercedes-Benz, since the automaker started making them in 1928.


Mercedes-Benz


Mercedes-Benz


The most powerful are at their most vulnerable when travelling by limo, and the impact of a car-borne assassination can be catastrophic: Witness Archduke Franz Ferdinand and the outbreak of the First World War. Leaders choose a Merc for its impregnability rather than its image. Former Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze survived two assassination attempts in his armoured S600: the first with a car bomb, the second with rocket-propelled grenades.


### Specs: 2027 Mercedes-Benz S680 Guard


**Price** : $800,000 (est’d)


**Powertrain** : 6.0-liter twin-turbocharged V-12; nine-speed automatic transmission


**Output** : 604 hp @ 4800 rpm; 612 lb-ft of torque @ 2000-4000 rpm


**Layout** : Front-engine, four-door, four-passenger, all-wheel-drive armored sedan


**Weight** : 9215 lbs


**0-to-60 mph** : 8.3 seconds


**EPA-Rated Fuel Economy** : Not currently available in the U.S.


**Competitors** : BMW 7 Protection


The current generation of dictator-spec Merc, the S680 Guard, is based on the seventh-generation W223 S-Class. It was heavily revised earlier this year, and since then we’ve both driven it and, more importantly, ridden in the back. Few ever will. Mercedes will vet you before it will sell you one. It won’t sell them at all in China, Russia, or certain other nations. It won’t disclose who buys them, or how many it will make, or how much they cost. There is no fixed price anyway: every Guard car is bespoke, and Mercedes will build yours with any legal and ethical extra you request. Wiring can be equipped to, after the fact, add other extras, which may not be.


Mercedes-Benz


Invisibility is this car’s first line of defense. As you approach it, it is almost indistinguishable from an ordinary, long-wheelbase, airport-specification S-Class, an impression reinforced by the modest, base-spec-looking wheels. The massively thicker glass with its deeper black frames is the only other giveaway.


Mercedes-Benz


Mercedes-Benz


Our test displayed a couple of other tells, ones that a Guard conveying someone of actual importance would not. The most obvious was the pair of front-mounted flags with ‘Guard’ emblazoned on them: not an option many will tick. The more subtle clue was the V12 badge on the flank and the S680 badge on the trunk. The Guard is the only non-Maybach S-Class that uses Mercedes’ 6-liter, 604-hp twin-turbo V-12 engine, and thus the only one to bear those badges. Your assassin is unlikely to be a Mercedes geek, but the rep from Mercedes’ Guard program confirmed that pretty much everyone deletes the badge anyway.


Mercedes-Benz


Mercedes-Benz


Mercedes-Benz


Mercedes-Benz


The Guard’s invisibility and impregnability are down to the fact that it was thoroughly and expensively engineered, in-house, by Mercedes-Benz. This happened alongside the development of the standard S-Class from the outset, and the Guard is built in a secure, dedicated facility at the Sindelfingen factory by specially vetted staff. According to the German Ballistics Authority, it is the only factory-built armored sedan to be rated to VR10—the highest possible civilian protection level. Both the bodywork and glass will withstand at least three 7.62x54mm explosive-tipped, armor-piercing rounds in a 20cm cluster, as well as the blast from a standard hand grenade. Protection from roadside IEDs requires military-grade armor, but you’d still have a far better chance of surviving in your Guard than your poor lackeys in the soft-skinned G-Wagen at the back of the convoy.


Mercedes is understandably coy about the precise details of how the car is armored, but if you run your hand under the sill, you can feel the thick composite blast shield. Only the passenger cell is armored, with the remainder of the car left unarmored to save weight. The doors weigh an astonishing 550 pounds each and require actuators to ensure you can open them if your car comes to a halt on an incline and you have to make a run for it. The windows alone weigh around 100 pounds and have a polycarbonate inner layer as a last defence against splintering. They can, optionally, be wound up or down hydraulically, with a pressure accumulator ensuring they will still move even if the car loses power. A tank with 900 liters of compressed oxygen provides fresh air in the event of a chemical attack, keeping the cabin under positive pressure. A fire extinguisher system can put out a blaze under the car, as well as in the engine bay. You can have a public address system, concealed blue lights, and a convoy light system which indicates to the protective service car inches off your tail whether you’re accelerating or decelerating even before the brake lights come on. The Mercedes can do plenty else that the automaker won’t discuss.


Mercedes-Benz


Mercedes-Benz


Mercedes-Benz


Mercedes-Benz


The Guard uses Michelin’s PAX run-flat system, in which metric-sized, asymmetric rims clamp the tire into place and have a solid polymer inner “tire” on which the car rests if the main rubber deflates. The same system was fitted to the original Bugatti Veyron and Rolls-Royce Phantom because it provided run-flat capabilities without the need for a stiff sidewall, thereby maintaining good ride quality. It was introduced in the year 2000 but largely phased out for production cars by the end of that decade because of the high cost of new tires and the near impossibility of finding anyone who could fit them. But that’s not a problem if a car is owned and maintained by a government, which can simply buy a stock of 20 mounted spares. In these circumstances, run-flats are essential; the ability to keep driving for another 20 miles is of great significance when the chief puncture risk is from bullets.


Mercedes-Benz


Once inside, it’s hard to tell the Guard apart from a standard S-Class. The armor and thicker glass don’t intrude into the cabin at all, nor does the glass distort the view out. In the rear, where it really counts, it’s still pure sybarism, with deeply reclining individual chairs, gorgeous quilted hides, super-soft pillows, and a fabulous Burmester audio system. *Thank you, generous taxpayer!* The switches controlling the extra gadgets are hidden behind the sliding panels in the central consoles.


Mercedes-Benz


Mercedes-Benz


We’ve driven a few of these heavily armored passenger cars before, and the feeling is quite unlike anything else on the road: that of an irresistible force overcoming an almost immovable object. This thing weighs 9215 pounds even before accounting for the driver, government aide, and tyrant wearing a long, heavy row of self-awarded medals and a gilded Colt 45 on his hip.


Mercedes-Benz


When driving, it’s best to start out slowly, respectful of the impact the extra mass will have on the dynamics, but also of the value and irreplaceability of what you’re driving. But you soon gain confidence. The 4Matic all-wheel drive system, Airmatic suspension, brakes and stability control have all, of course, been factory-tuned to suit the weight. The ride is suitably imperious, ironing flat any road surface imperfections. The steering takes its time to respond off-center; there’s more lean than usual when cornering, and you can feel that the car wants to push its nose wide. Those 245-section tires would be plainly challenged by the weight in more extreme driving. But even on our fairly spirited drive on a country road circuit at Mercedes’ usually secret Immendingen test track, the Guard went where it was ordered.


Mercedes-Benz


At 8.3 seconds, the Guard takes almost twice as long to get to 60 mph as a standard S-Class, but it doesn’t feel slow. In normal, waving-at-the-crowds driving, it is almost EV-silent. But the noise you get when you extend that V-12 is just glorious: sonorous and multi-cylindric. It’s just a pity that if your driver ever *has* to give it full gas, it means you’re being assailed and might not appreciate the musicality of the motor in that moment.


## 2027 Mercedes-Benz S680 Guard


**Highs** : The de facto choice for royalty, presidents, prime ministers, and despots; no factory civilian vehicle is more bulletproof.


**Lows** : Won’t win a drag race. Probably thirsty enough that you want to make sure your country has oil reserves.


**Takeaway** : The ride of the 0.00001 percent contains capabilities you never hope to need.
